Russia? EA-Times Radio VideoCast: Ukraine Brings The War to Russia’s Doorstep Friday’s Coverage: Zelensky Under Pressure Over Firing of Defense Minister Fedorov UPDATE 1121 GMT: Eleven civilians were murdered and 62 injured by Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day. Air defenses intercepted only one of seven missiles and 69 of 90 drones launched by Russia overnight. Missiles and UAVs struck 19 locations. The Odesa region was again the primary target, with a 77-year-old man slain. A Russian strike damaged a Marshall Islands-flagged civilian vessel. Four injured crew were among 17 evacuated. In the Kherson region in the south, three people were murdered and 18 injured in attacks on 41 settlements. In the neighboring Zaporizhzhia region, one civilian was killed and two injured, including a child. In the Donetsk region in the east, three people were murdered and eight wounded. In the Dnipropetrovsk region in the southeast, a 48-year-old man was killed and nine people injured. In the Kharkiv region in the northeast, two people were slain and 17 injured, including five children, in attacks on Kharkiv city and 29 other settlements. Casualties were also recorded in the Chernihiv and Sumy regions. UPDATE 0617 GMT: One civilian was murdered and eight injured, including two children aged 7 and 2, by a Russian strike on a passenger vehicle in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine on Friday. UPDATE 0607 GMT: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces struck another 13 Russian shadow fleet vessels overnight: eight dry cargo ships, one oil tanker, one gas carrier, one tugboat, and two floating cranes. Since July 6, Ukraine has hit 172 vessels, 118 in the Sea of Azov and 54 in the Black Sea. ORIGINAL ENTRY: Larger crowds turned out on Friday across Ukraine for the second day of protests over President Volodymyr Zelensky’s dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Several thousand people gathered in the capital Kyiv and other cities calling for the reinstatement of Fedorov, who has been hailed for innovations turning the tide against Russia’s invasion this year. Zelensky said he “understands, hears, and responds” to public concerns. Referring to the dispute between Fedorov and military commander-in-chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrski, he said he was forced “to choose between sides [when] what I want most is unity”. However, Zelensky gave no sign of reversing his decision. Instead, he posted about a meeting on Friday with Fedorov’s proposed replacement, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko. I met with Ihor Klymenko. I am grateful to him for his work within the Ministry of Internal Affairs. There have been many difficult challenges, and the response has always been effective. Ihor Klymenko will continue working for Ukraine in the field of protecting our state and… pic.twitter.com/nUgrvBNrRS — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) July 17, 2026 Zelensky Tries To Repair Relations With Poland The President tried to repair a rift with Poland, sparked by his decision ⁠in May to name a Ukrainian army unit in honour of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which killed tens of thousands of Poles in World War II. Zelensky posted after a meeting on Ukrainian policy towards its neighbor that “there will be decisions on the diplomatic track”. Ukrainian archives on the Volyn massacre in summer 1943 will be opened, and permits will be granted for searches and exhumations. Support will be given to Ukrainian institutes for “expanding dialogue” with Polish counterparts. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk responded that Warsaw is “ready for a serious and friendly dialogue on the issues that unite us and those that divide us”. https://nineoclock.ro/eturia-exceeds-e20.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Eturia exceeds €20 million in sales in the first half of the year Tourist numbers increased by nearly 29%, while demand is diversifying towards premium holidays, complex tours and themed experiences By Mihai Manea , Publisher, Nine O’Clock / Social Media: LinkedIn | Facebook | Instagram Eturia Group closed the first six months of the year with sales exceeding €20 million, up approximately 7% compared with the same period in 2025. The results confirm Romanians’ continued interest in tailor-made travel and long-haul destinations, as well as Eturia’s development amid increasingly diverse demand for complex tours, premium holidays and themed experiences. In the first half of the year, approximately 10,500 tourists travelled with Eturia, nearly 29% more than during the same period of the previous year. The destinations recording the highest demand included the Maldives, China, Australia, the Dominican Republic and Thailand. These preferences point to a diversified market, in which relaxing stays in exotic destinations are complemented by cultural journeys, exploration tours and long-distance itineraries. “The growth recorded during the first six months confirms that Eturia is developing on solid foundations and that our model, built around specialised consultancy and destination expertise, meets the current expectations of travellers. We remain focused on strengthening our portfolio, developing the premium segment and expanding the range of products that offer clients greater flexibility, predictability and access to carefully selected experiences,” said Sorin Stoica, CEO and Founder of Eturia. Eturia exceeds €20 million in sales in the first half of the year The Maldives and Thailand remain leading exotic destinations, while China and Australia attract travellers interested in exploration The Maldives continues to be one of the preferred choices for premium holidays, relaxation and personalised services, while Thailand maintains its appeal through its varied offering of beaches, cultural experiences, gastronomy and itineraries adapted to different types of travellers. At the same time, China and Australia highlight the growing interest in destinations that require more extensive planning and offer cultural and exploration-based experiences. The Dominican Republic completes the list of preferred destinations, being chosen primarily for exotic stays and premium services. The diversity of selected destinations shows that travellers’ preferences are expanding beyond traditional relaxation holidays. An increasing number of requests are focused on holidays that include local experiences, exploration and activities adapted to each traveller’s individual style. More than 80 escorted groups operated during the first six months Escorted group travel continues to represent an important segment for Eturia. More than 80 groups were operated during the first six months of the year, indicating that this format remains relevant for travellers seeking a well-organised experience without giving up the authenticity of discovering a destination. Group products are particularly attractive due to the balance they offer between comfort, access to expertise and carefully designed itineraries. The presence of a tour escort provides travellers with an additional level of predictability and support, particularly in the case of complex tours or long-haul destinations. At the same time, this format facilitates access to complex routes, local activities and cultural experiences that may be more difficult to organise independently. Demand is evolving from choosing a destination to creating a personal experience Data from the first part of the year indicates a diversification in the way Romanians choose their holidays. Alongside established exotic stays, interest is increasing in complex tours, long-haul travel and premium or luxury products. An increasingly visible trend is the preference for holidays developed around personal interests and objectives. Wellbeing, adventure, culture and exploration are becoming important criteria in the decision-making process, while the destination itself represents only the starting point in building the itinerary. Travellers are looking for programmes adapted to their own pace and travel style, ranging from relaxing stays and active routes to cultural experiences and in-depth exploration of a region. In this context, personalisation and specialised consultancy are playing an increasingly important role in the holiday selection process. In the spring of 1968, when Kerala was given the opportunity to inaugurate a retrospective of Soviet films, the communist government led by EMS Namboodiripad seized it unreservedly. At a time when India was being courted by the Cold War superpowers, Kerala was one state that overwhelmingly leaned towards Moscow rather than Washington DC. Nine Russian films were screened in Trivandrum and other parts of the state, beginning with Sergei Eisenstein’s 1925 silent epic Battleship Potemkin . For Kerala, the retrospective was an opportunity to showcase a cinema that was closely associated with the state’s political culture. For Moscow, it was part of a much longer effort to make Soviet cinema – and the system it represented – more attractive to Indian audiences. The staging of the retrospective, which commemorated 50 years of Soviet cinema, was the result of years of Soviet efforts to popularise Russian films in a country where the post-colonial elite could watch and easily comprehend English films. The Soviets were acutely aware that the Americans could reach a significant section of Indians through Hollywood since there was no language barrier, giving them an advantage in promoting Western capitalism over Russian communism. “The USSR tried its best to convince Indians that a socialist country could be a superpower and that Indians too could achieve the same level of development if they took the Communist path,” historian Severyan Dyakonov wrote in his 2015 master’s thesis at Concordia University in Montreal, Canada. To overcome the language barrier, and reach a wider audience, Moscow initially explored dubbing Russian films into Indian language. The Soviets hoped this would replicate the massive popularity that Indian films, particularly those directed by and starring Raj Kapoor, had achieved in the Soviet Union after being dubbed in Russian. However, the process proved to be far too expensive. The relationship between the two film industries gained new momentum in the early 1960s, when the Sino-Soviet split damaged relations between Moscow and Beijing and the Russians made a strong attempt to expand film cooperation with India. A poster of 'Battleship Potemkin'. At the time, a special licence was required for countries to distribute their films in India. From 1960, this licence depended on the reciprocal exchange of films, according to Dyakonov. This enabled the Soviets to sell as many films as they bought from India. “The reciprocal film exchange was a strategy of the Indian government to reach new markets for its own film industry,” Dyakonov added. Oscar winners like Sergei Bondarchuk’s War and Peace and Destiny of a Man found their way to Indian cinemas with English subtitles. But it was in 1967 that Moscow made a more ambitious attempt to bring Soviet cinema to India: the Soviet government reached out to the National Film Archives of India in Poona to organise a Soviet film retrospective. Cultural diplomacy When the National Film Archives agreed to stage the festival, the Soviets initially focused on two main themes: the Second World War, or the Great Patriotic War as they called it, and socialism. One Soviet classic extolling the values of socialism was Mother , a 1926 film directed by Vsevolod Pudovkin and adapted from Maxim Gorky’s popular novel of the same name. But the organisers in India wanted a wider picture of Soviet cinema. When the National Film Archives shared the potential list of films with the Federation of Film Societies of India, its assistant secretary, Basu Chatterjee, who would later become an award-winning director, called for films from the various centres of production across the USSR. “For example, Good Morning, This is I (Armenia), Contest (Turkmenia), Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors (Ukraine) and White Caravan (Georgia),” he wrote in a letter to the National Film Archives. “Only The Two from Latvia is included in the current list.” Chatterjee also argued that films such as Bondarchuk’s Destiny of a Man , which had already been screened in India, did not need to be included. A final list of 15 films was agreed upon, and the Federation of Film Societies agreed to try to also get them screened in smaller towns, where audiences had little access to international cinema. The logistics of moving the films across India were almost as important as the selection itself. In February 1968, the 35mm prints of the 15 chosen films were sent to Santa Cruz airport in Bombay, with the government requesting customs to clear them without collecting duties. A poster of 'Mother'. Credit: Wikimedia Commons [Public Domain]. Once the prints were with the National Film Archives, assistant curator PK Nair wrote to the Federation of Film Societies to ensure they were not damaged while being transported across India by rail. “We have to return the prints to the Russian Archive in the same good condition,” Nair wrote in a letter. “As such, I would request you to instruct all societies to take utmost care of the prints. Every precaution has to be taken to see that the prints are not even slightly damaged.” There was another issue to settle before the films could travel: censorship. Satyajit Ray, who was the president of the Federation of Film Societies, successfully appealed to the government not to censor any of the films that were going to be screened at the festival. This was significant. In the 1950s and 1960s, Indian censors had refused to clear several Soviet films, including documentary reels such as In Budapest and Aggression Against Egypt . “ In Budapest was likely censored because India openly criticised the USSR for its intervention in Hungary in 1956,” Dyakonov wrote. “It is not clear why the film on the Suez Crisis of 1956 was banned because the official position of India was close to the one of the Soviet Union.” Three films based on Gorky novels, including Pudovkin’s Mother , had also been banned by Indian censors in the 1950s for reasons that remain unclear. All three were included in the set screened across India during the 1968 retrospective. The National Film Archives and the Federation of Film Societies decided to take the films to Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The films were either dubbed in English or had English subtitles, effectively limiting their reach to the country’s educated elite. They were initially loaned to India for a period of four months. But the response would soon persuade the National Film Archives to ask for more time. Soft power The retrospective came at a time when India’s cultural ties with the Soviet Union were deepening. In October 1968, a large Indian delegation was invited to the inaugural Tashkent International Film Festival, launched as the Festival of Asian and African Countries. Since Indian films were not censored in the Soviet Union, the average Soviet citizen had a better idea of India than Indians did of the Soviet Union. Many in India believed the Soviet Union was a scientific superpower after festival screenings in 1959 of films about the Leningrad Metro, oil exploration in the Caspian Sea and the peaceful use of nuclear energy in the USSR. A poster of the 1930 film 'Earth'. Films about the Bolshevik Revolution, however, had rarely been screened in India before the 1968 retrospective. When those films finally reached Indian audiences, the response was strong outside the major cities. Films dealing with the revolution were well received in smaller towns such as Burhanpur, Quilon and Srivilliputhur. The screenings also sparked renewed interest in Gorky’s works in Kerala, generating fresh demand for Malayalam translations. The response was strong enough for the National Film Archives to ask the Soviets to let them keep the prints in India for well over a year. Moscow was more than happy to oblige. The films continued to travel. Alexander Dovzhenko’s 1930 film Earth , about the collectivisation of agriculture, was screened in Calicut in March 1969. In a letter to the National Film Archives, MC Ramavarma Raja, patron of the Calicut Film Society, called the film “poetry in celluloid”. He also praised the other Soviet film screened in the city, Chapaev , a 1934 film about the Russian Civil War. Some films were screened by the Poona University Russian Association at the Ranade Institute. In November 1969, they found their way to West Bengal, where Cine Central, Calcutta, screened them as part of celebrations marking the 52nd anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution. The rector of Patrice Lumumba Peoples’ Friendship University presided over the function. While many Indians were disappointed with the Soviet role in mediating the Tashkent peace agreement between India and Pakistan after the 1965 war, by the end of the decade Moscow and New Delhi were moving closer diplomatically. The Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation, signed in August 1971, paved the way for closer strategic and diplomatic cooperation, including Soviet backing for India during the Bangladesh Liberation War. Cultural ties also flourished during the peak of the Leonid Brezhnev era, with Soviet films regularly screened at festivals and on university campuses. They could never compete with the spectacle and budgets of Hollywood, but they did reach the audience Moscow had been trying to cultivate in India for decades. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters Poland Kraków shooting suspect who killed six has died, say police in Poland Terrorism investigation continues after 24-year-old opened fire in market square, leaving 16 injured Angela Giuffrida and agencies Mon 9 Nov 2026 05.22 EST First published on Mon 9 Nov 2026 01.32 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A gunman who killed six people, including a British man, and injured 16 in a rare mass shooting in a busy market square in Kraków has died in hospital, Polish police said. The suspect, a 24-year-old Polish national who has not yet been officially named, opened fire in the city’s main square on Saturday afternoon in an attack that a government minister said was probably influenced by far-right ideologies. He was wounded during a shootout with police and taken to hospital in a critical condition. “We would like to inform you that the perpetrator of the tragic events died in hospital early this morning,” Małopolska police wrote on X on Monday. Soon after the attack, the bodies of the gunman’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds. Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation, which the justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said would continue despite the gunman’s death and would aim to establish if he acted alone or was inspired by any group. However, he called for “restraint” after the interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said on Saturday that the gunman was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views. “Evidence is ​being collected, ​but I will not ​show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” ​Żurek told Radio ‌Zet. Wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said. Karolina Gałecka, an ⁠interior ministry spokesperson, told radio TOK FM ​on ​Monday: “There ​were many different emblems on the perpetrator’s clothing that have been partially examined and interpreted. “These patches were ​associated with various motifs that ​are currently ‌being analysed ​by ​specialists,” she added, declining to comment further as the investigation was ongoing. The shooting has shocked a country that was considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online. Among the six victims were a 32-year-old British man and an Austrian woman aged 51. The other four victims were Polish nationals. Of the 16 injured, 15 were in a stable condition as of late Sunday, including two police officers who were brought out of medically induced comas earlier in the day. Five of the injured were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia. Two police officers hailed as heroes for confronting Kraków gunman Read more Police said the suspect, who had no criminal record and held a firearms licence, initially continued shooting even after he was wounded by police during the exchange of fire. The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties. Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21. Mourners have left candles in tribute to the victims in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast during two days of national mourning, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.
